summary:
Kirov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia in full. The sources reviewed identify no deviation in this oblast material enough to assess separately, so a trans visitor should expect the national position to apply without local modification.

Since 2023, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned across Russia, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised, but that distinction offers little protection given the expression offences below.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, rising to as much as four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law reaches any public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners found guilty of violating it may be arrested, held for up to 15 days and then deported, and displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is itself treated as a crime.

Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, alleged participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal, brought for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Official travel advisories reflect this. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, advises against all travel, and carries warnings directed specifically at LGBT travellers, noting that foreign nationals who violate the propaganda law face arrest, detention and deportation.

Enforcement is documented at volume as well as in severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those laws bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the preceding two years. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photography, with at least two further venues raided the same night. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is independently documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern of enforcement described by national outlets is one of raids, arrests and extremism charges rather than isolated prosecutions, and it intensified sharply after the 2023 designation. A traveller in Kirov Oblast should read the national figures as the operative environment even though no oblast-specific incident appears in the sources.

Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia in response to the extremism designation, which indicates that external bodies treat the risk as grounds for departure rather than internal relocation.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. The conversion-therapy detention documented by BBC Russian involved relatives as the agents of coercion, so risk in this setting is not confined to state action.
localsOnly:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

That same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Residents considering departure should note that the national legal position applies identically inside Kirov Oblast: no pathway exists to change a legal gender marker, to obtain gender-affirming care, or to enter a same-sex marriage, and public expression supportive of gender transition is itself an offence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement actions, raids, prosecutions or police conduct specific to Kirov Oblast, so the oblast-level picture is unresolved rather than clear. The assessment here rests on national sources applied to this jurisdiction.

The inventory does not establish whether any Kirov Oblast municipal or regional instrument adds obligations beyond the national statutes, nor whether local authorities have issued guidance affecting LGBT venues, events or documents. Both points remain unsourced.

Facility availability for transgender visitors in Kirov Oblast, including competent medical care and safe accommodation, is not covered by any source reviewed and is unresolved.

Reports of deaths in pretrial detention and of conversion-therapy detention are documented at national level with dates and outcomes as stated, but their frequency in this oblast is not sourced.
